characters: Yaa: a girl of nine, curious and determined, with a notebook.
Kofi: her younger brother, cheerful and casual.
Auntie Akosua and Mr Mensah: helpful neighbours.

narrationPlan.voice: Clear, lively storyteller (en-GH or en-GB); a curious, determined girl’s voice for Yaa without imitating a child.
notes: Names go through the pronunciation dictionary (unverified).

music: Optional gentle rain ambience on the first pages; off by default. Not created.
culturalNotes: The drain, flooded lane and recycling collection are common in many Ghanaian towns; confirm local recycling practice before the final version (is plastic actually collected locally?).
Names are Akan; pronunciation needs native review.
reviewQuestions: Is the recycling description accurate for most schools (is collection available)?
Is Yaa leading the neighbours (an adult-led community) plausible, or should an adult guide her more explicitly?
Is the safety of children working at a drain addressed (gloves, adult supervision)? Consider adding a line about an adult supervising.

pages.brief: Morning after rain, a flooded lane in a Ghanaian neighbourhood, Yaa at the doorway, shoes afloat. Surprised, not frightened.
pages.narration: Wide-eyed and lively; slow on "a brown river".

pages.brief: Yaa crouching to look, Kofi shrugging behind her; curiosity in her face.
pages.narration: Curious, a little determined. Kofi casual.

pages.brief: Yaa at the edge of an open concrete drain, water backed up in front of it, a clear sense of a blockage.
pages.narration: Building curiosity; the "crowd at a gate" image is playful.

pages.brief: Close view into the drain full of plastic bottles, sachets, bags and mud (no brand names or readable text). Yaa’s thoughtful face.
Yaa at a table with a hand-drawn lane map (simple marks and numbers only), pencil in hand, a sense of focus.
pages.narration: Clear, factual; clearly say the number forty-two.

pages.brief: A friendly group of neighbours of different ages at the drain with brooms, gloves and a wheelbarrow. Community energy.
pages.narration: Warm, building; each neighbour named clearly.

pages.brief: The team sorting plastic into labelled piles (symbols, no text) and water starting to flow in the drain; light, hopeful.
pages.narration: Energetic, then a soft sense of release at the gurgle.

pages.brief: The flow in the cleared drain, the lane reappearing, Kofi cheering; Yaa smiling but thoughtful.
pages.narration: Joyful, then a quieter turn on the last line.

pages.brief: Yaa speaking at assembly in front of classmates in uniform; head teacher smiling; confident but not showy.
The Clean Lane Club by the clean drain with a simple chart (numbers falling, no readable words), dry lane, sunshine.
pages.narration: Steady, satisfied, a smile at the end; clear on "forty-two to six".

teacherGuide.overview: A girl investigates why the lane floods, counts the rubbish, leads her community to clear the drain and starts a school club that tracks the improvement with numbers. Models the scientific habit of observing, counting and checking.
learningGoals: Explain how a blocked drain causes flooding.
Use counting and subtraction to show a change over time.
Describe one small action that protects the local environment.

subjectLinks.subject: Science
subjectLinks.link: Water, rain and drainage; observing and recording.

subjectLinks.subject: Mathematics
subjectLinks.link: Counting, subtraction, reading a simple chart.

subjectLinks.subject: Our World Our People / Social Studies
subjectLinks.link: Community action and caring for the environment.

beforeReading: Ask: "What happens to rainwater after it falls on our school?"
Look at a photo or drawing of a drain (use a local one).
whileReading: Pause after page 4 and ask learners to explain, in a sentence, why the water was stuck.
After page 5, ask what Yaa should do next.
afterReading: Do a 10-minute rubbish count of a safe area at school and chart it.
Compare with a count a week later.
discussion: Why did Yaa count the rubbish instead of just clearing it?
Why did some neighbours say they were too busy? How did Yaa persuade them?
What could our class do that is like the Clean Lane Club?
reflection: What problem near your home or school could you investigate like Yaa?
Who would you ask to help you?

mathsExtension.task: Weekly counts were 42, 30, 18, 9 and 6. How many fewer is the last than the first? Which week saw the biggest drop?
mathsExtension.answer: 36 fewer. The biggest drop is from 42 to 30 (12) and from 30 to 18 (12): both are 12.

support: Count with objects first; use a number line to subtract.
stretch: Draw a bar chart of the weekly counts and write two sentences about it.

culturalNotes: Yaa is an Akan day name for a girl born on Thursday, Kofi for a boy born on Friday and Akosua for a girl born on Sunday; Mensah is a family name. A native speaker should verify pronunciation.
localiseThis: Replace the drain, stream and market details with what learners see locally; do not use a real named community without permission.

pronunciation.guidance: a single long "YAAH" (the double a marks a long vowel).
reviewerNotes: Confirm vowel length; engines may shorten it to "ya".
Confirm the vowel in the first syllable (oh vs aw).

pronunciation.guidance: "ah-KOH-swah"; a three-syllable "ah-KOH-soo-ah" may be more accurate.
reviewerNotes: Two or three syllables at the end? Please decide.
